editorial_notice: These are explanations and methodological connections, not new mathematical results or independent verification. Research status is governed by the canonical ledgers.

guides.summary: How colouring, graph minors and exact certificates meet.
guides.intuition: Colouring asks how many colours are needed so that adjacent vertices differ. A graph minor is obtained by deleting vertices or edges and contracting edges. Hadwiger asks whether needing k colours always forces the complete graph K_k to appear as a minor. Finding a large clique directly is not required: contraction can reveal structure that was not visible as a subgraph.
guides.obstacle: Finite searches over small graphs reproduce known cases, not the unsettled frontier. The campaign records that the conjecture is proved through k = 6, while a meaningful k = 7 test needs much larger graphs and certified chromatic lower bounds. A 2026 claimed resolution remains under review.
guides.meaningful_check: A genuine counterexample would need two independent parts: a certified lower bound on chromatic number, and an exhaustive certificate excluding the corresponding complete-graph minor. A restricted positive theorem instead needs a precisely specified new graph class and an independent prior-art check.

bridges.reason: Both problems use graph search and independently checkable certificates, but one studies undirected minors and the other directed cycles.
Symmetry reduction can save exhaustive work in both projects; a computational shortcut is not a logical implication between conjectures.

guides.summary: Why many outgoing edges should force a short directed cycle.
guides.intuition: Imagine a directed network with n vertices where every vertex sends edges to at least r others. The conjecture predicts a directed cycle of length at most ceil(n/r). The direction of every edge matters: an undirected loop is not enough. The challenge is to turn a local outdegree condition into a universal guarantee about a short directed circuit.
guides.obstacle: The project has independently testable finite cases and mathematical reductions, but its campaign records an external fixed-r = 6 proof corpus that has not been independently replayed here. Even accepting one fixed-r result would not by itself prove the unrestricted conjecture.
guides.meaningful_check: For a bounded case, check the precise reduction, enumerate or certify the remaining candidates, and independently verify the cycle condition or unsatisfiability certificate. Record the exact n and r covered; do not promote a finite exclusion into a general proof.

bridges.reason: Both ask global structural questions about graphs and rely on exact graph certificates; the invariants and proof obligations differ.
Canonicalization and symmetry-aware enumeration are shared computational techniques, not evidence that either conjecture implies the other.

guides.summary: A deceptively simple half-frequency claim about families of sets.
guides.intuition: A family of sets is union-closed if the union of any two of its members is also a member. Frankl asks whether some element occurs in at least half the sets of every finite nontrivial such family. For example, the family { {1}, {2}, {1,2} } is union-closed, and each element appears in two of its three members.
guides.obstacle: A direct search grows doubly exponentially with the ground-set size. The project's n = 4 checks and symmetry-class counts are reproducible finite evidence; they cannot establish the statement for arbitrary families. Structural reductions and entropy arguments are separate mathematical avenues requiring their own proof.
guides.meaningful_check: A counterexample must list an exact finite union-closed family and verify that every element appears in strictly fewer than half its sets. For positive progress, prove a genuinely new restricted lemma or a rigorously checked reduction beyond the known finite census.

bridges.reason: Canonical representatives help avoid repeated cases in finite search, though the objects are set families rather than graphs.
Both need careful separation of verified finite instances from unrestricted universal statements.
